newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Italy deals Nigerian gas project serious blow.
newsitem.headline: Italy deals Nigerian gas project serious blow.

text.p: Nigeria's $4 billion project to liquefy and export its natural gas suffered a serious blow on Tuesday when the Italian state power firm that should have been the main importer cancelled a contract to buy the gas.

Enel linked its decision to its abandonment for technical, economic and environmental reasons of its own project to construct a terminal at Montalto di Castro, north of Rome, to receive the Nigerian gas.

Nigerian Liquefied Natural Gas Limited (NLNG), the company implementing the project, put a brave face to the cancellation, saying the project would go ahead and immediately launched an action for compensation.

"NLNG regrets Enel's conduct," the Nigerian LNG company (NLNG) said in a statement, adding "NLNG has initiated arbitration proceedings in Switzerland to obtain compensation from Enel for all losses resulting from Enel's breach of contract," it added.
Enel signed the contract in November and was to receive the first cargo of Nigerian LNG in the third quarter of 1999.
The Nigerian project is to produce 7.2 billion cubic metres of LNG per year from a plant projected to come on stream in 1999. Enel was to take 3.5 billion cubic metres of the output annually.
NLNG said the compensation was yet to be quantified but was likely to be substantial.
"The value of the contract is estimated over its 22.5 years life to be at least US$12 billion," it said.
Partners in the project are the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation, Shell Gas BV, Elf Aquitaine and Italy's Agip SpA.
Long-term supply contracts have been signed with Enargas of Spain and Gaz de France.
Nigeria said sales to other buyers would not be affected.
Work on the project has been at full blast this year in the Bonny in the oil-producing southeastern Nigeria.

The project came under threat last year when international lobby groups piled pressure on the partners to abandon the project over Nigeria's hanging of nine minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa for murder.
The $4 billion project is the biggest in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Nigeria has muted the idea of the LNG plant for 25 years.
NLNG said Enel first entered into the purchase contract in 1992 and its commitment was "a crucial consideration in the decision by shareholders in the NLNG to proceed with the LNG project."
